claim: Quorum sensing (QS) is a cell-cell communication process that bacteria use to orchestrate collective behaviors.
source: Quorum sensing (QS) is a cell–cell communication process that bacteria use to orchestrate collective behaviors.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about quorum sensing that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: QS relies on the production, release, and group-level detection of molecules called autoinducers.
source: QS relies on the production, release, and group-level detection of molecules called autoinducers (reviewed in Papenfort and Bassler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: At low cell density (LCD), when autoinducer concentration is low, QS promotes gene expression programs that benefit individual bacteria.
source: At low cell density (LCD), when autoinducer concentration is low, QS promotes gene expression programs that benefit individual bacteria.
evidence: This is a general statement about QS behavior that draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: At high cell density (HCD), when autoinducer concentration exceeds the threshold required for detection, QS drives gene expression programs beneficial to the community.
source: At high cell density (HCD), when autoinducer concentration exceeds the threshold required for detection, QS drives gene expression programs beneficial to the community.
evidence: This is a general statement about QS behavior that draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Vibrio cholerae is the etiological agent of the disease cholera.
source: Vibrio cholerae is the etiological agent of the disease cholera.
evidence: This is an established fact in microbiology and infectious disease.

claim: In V. cholerae, QS controls virulence factor production and biofilm formation.
source: In V. cholerae, QS controls virulence factor production and biofilm formation (Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Miller et al., 2002; Papenfort and Bassler, 2016; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003; Zhu et al., 2002) (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: V. cholerae relies on two major autoinducers: CAI-1, an intra-genus-specific autoinducer, and AI-2, an autoinducer broadly conserved across bacteria and used for inter-species communication.
source: V. cholerae relies on two major autoinducers: CAI-1, an intra-genus-specific autoinducer (Higgins et al., 2007; Kelly et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2002), and AI-2, an autoinducer broadly conserved across bacteria and used for inter-species communication (Chen et al., 2002; Schauder et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The CAI-1 and AI-2 receptors are CqsS and LuxPQ, respectively.
source: The CAI-1 and AI-2 receptors are CqsS and LuxPQ, respectively (Bassler et al., 1994; Miller et al., 2002; Neiditch et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the absence of autoinducer, CqsS and LuxPQ act as kinases funneling phosphate through an integrator protein, LuxU, to LuxO, the shared response regulator protein.
source: In the absence of autoinducer, CqsS and LuxPQ act as kinases funneling phosphate through an integrator protein, LuxU, to LuxO, the shared response regulator protein (Freeman and Bassler, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Phosphorylated LuxO activates transcription of genes encoding four small RNAs: Qrr-1 to Qrr-4.
source: Phosphorylated LuxO activates transcription of genes encoding four small RNAs: Qrr-1 to Qrr-4 (Lenz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Qrr1-4 activate translation of AphA and repress translation of HapR; respectively the master LCD and master HCD QS regulators.
source: Qrr1-4 activate translation of AphA and repress translation of HapR; respectively the master LCD and master HCD QS regulators (Lenz et al., 2004; Rutherford et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: At LCD, AphA is made and HapR is not, and V. cholerae cells act as individuals.
source: Thus, at LCD, AphA is made and HapR is not, and V. cholerae cells act as individuals (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is an inference from the described regulatory pathway.

claim: When bound to their cognate autoinducers, which occurs at HCD, CqsS and LuxPQ switch from acting as kinases to acting as phosphatases, dephosphorylating LuxO, via LuxU.
source: When bound to their cognate autoinducers, which occurs at HCD, CqsS and LuxPQ switch from acting as kinases to acting as phosphatases, dephosphorylating LuxO, via LuxU.
evidence: This is a description of the molecular mechanism of QS signaling based on established knowledge.

claim: Dephosphorylated LuxO is inactive, so transcription of qrr1-4 does not occur.
source: Dephosphorylated LuxO is inactive, so transcription of qrr1-4 does not occur.
evidence: This is an inference from the described regulatory mechanism.

claim: In the absence of the Qrr sRNAs, activation of AphA translation ceases and HapR translation is no longer repressed.
source: In the absence of the Qrr sRNAs, activation of AphA translation ceases and HapR translation is no longer repressed.
evidence: This is an inference from the described regulatory mechanism.

claim: At HCD, HapR is made and AphA is not, and V. cholerae cells engage in group behaviors.
source: Thus, HapR is made and AphA is not, and V. cholerae cells engage in group behaviors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and is an inference from the described regulatory pathway.

claim: Two other QS receptors, CqsR and VpsS, with unknown ligands, also convey information into the QS circuit via LuxU.
source: Two other QS receptors, CqsR and VpsS, with unknown ligands, also convey information into the QS circuit via LuxU (Jung et al., 2015; Shikuma et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: In V. cholerae, QS controls the formation of surface-bound multicellular communities called biofilms.
source: In V. cholerae, QS controls the formation of surface-bound multicellular communities called biofilms (Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Teschler et al., 2015; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: AphA promotes and HapR represses the production of four components required for biofilm formation: vibrio polysaccharide (VPS) and three matrix proteins, RbmA, Bap1, and RbmC.
source: Specifically, AphA promotes and HapR represses the production of four components required for biofilm formation: vibrio polysaccharide (VPS) and three matrix proteins, RbmA, Bap1, and RbmC (Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Yang et al., 2010; Yildiz et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: V. cholerae forms biofilms at LCD and disperses from them at HCD.
source: The result of this regulatory arrangement is that V. cholerae forms biofilms at LCD and disperses from them at HCD (Miller et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2017; Teschler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Extracellular DNA (eDNA) contributes to V. cholerae biofilm formation.
source: Extracellular DNA (eDNA) also contributes to V. cholerae biofilm formation (Seper et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: eDNA levels are regulated by the activity of two extracellular nucleases: Xds and Dns, the latter of which is repressed at HCD by HapR.
source: eDNA levels are regulated by the activity of two extracellular nucleases: Xds and Dns, the latter of which is repressed at HCD by HapR (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The lifecycle of V. cholerae requires transitions between the marine environment and the human host.
source: The lifecycle of V. cholerae requires transitions between the marine environment and the human host (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: In both the marine environment and the human host, biofilm formation and dispersal appear to occur.
source: In both niches, biofilm formation and dispersal appear to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described lifecycle of V. cholerae.

claim: In the marine environment, V. cholerae associates with chitin, a major component of transient nutrient sources such as marine snow.
source: Specifically, in the marine environment, V. cholerae associates with chitin, a major component of transient nutrient sources such as marine snow (Huq et al., 1983; Pruzzo et al., 2008; Yawata et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: To successfully adapt to the disappearance of marine snow upon consumption, V. cholerae must be able to transition between the surface-associated state and the planktonic state.
source: To successfully adapt to the disappearance of marine snow upon consumption, V. cholerae must be able to transition between the surface-associated state and the planktonic state.
evidence: This is an inference about the ecological requirements of V. cholerae.

claim: Infections in humans occur when contaminated water or food containing planktonic and/or aggregates of V. cholerae cells is ingested.
source: Infections in humans occur when contaminated water or food containing planktonic and/or aggregates of V. cholerae cells is ingested.
evidence: This is a statement about the mode of V. cholerae transmission based on established knowledge.

claim: Early in human infection, V. cholerae cells, after passaging through the stomach, transit from the lumen of the small intestine through the mucosal layer to the epithelial surface.
source: Early in human infection, V. cholerae cells, after passaging through the stomach, transit from the lumen of the small intestine through the mucosal layer to the epithelial surface (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Both motility and chemotaxis are reported to play roles in V. cholerae transit through the mucosal layer, suggesting that cells exist in the planktonic state as they make this transition.
source: Both motility and chemotaxis are reported to play roles in this process suggesting that cells exist in the planktonic state as they make this transition (Butler and Camilli, 2005; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and includes an inference about cell state.

claim: At the epithelial surface, V. cholerae represses motility, forms surface microcolonies, and activates its virulence program.
source: At the epithelial surface, V. cholerae represses motility, forms surface microcolonies, and activates its virulence program (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015; Matson et al., 2007; Millet et al., 2014; Watnick et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Virulence factors, including the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) and cholera toxin (CT), are produced at LCD.
source: Virulence factors, including the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) and cholera toxin (CT), are produced at LCD.
evidence: This is a statement about the regulation of virulence factors based on established knowledge.

claim: CT causes severe diarrhea characteristic of the disease cholera.
source: CT causes severe diarrhea characteristic of the disease cholera (Matson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Later in infection, at HCD, HapR represses virulence factor production.
source: Later in infection, at HCD, HapR represses virulence factor production (Miller et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: HapR, together with RpoS, launches a mucosal escape program.
source: and HapR, together with RpoS, launches a mucosal escape program (Nielsen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: HapR activates expression of hapA, encoding the HapA mucinase, reported to contribute to the host-escape process.
source: Specifically in the case of QS, HapR activates expression of hapA, encoding the HapA mucinase, reported to contribute to the host-escape process (Booth et al., 1983; Silva et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: V. cholerae is shed back into the environment either as planktonic cells or as multicellular aggregates.
source: V. cholerae is shed back into the environment either as planktonic cells or as multicellular aggregates (Faruque et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Elegant work has defined the mechanisms underlying V. cholerae biofilm formation on surfaces.
source: Elegant work has defined the mechanisms underlying V. cholerae biofilm formation on surfaces (Absalon et al., 2011; Berk et al., 2012; Fong et al., 2017; Fong et al., 2010; Watnick et al., 1999; Yan et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Relatively little attention has been paid to whether V. cholerae forms communities in the absence of surfaces.
source: however, relatively little attention has been paid to whether V. cholerae forms communities in the absence of surfaces.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature.

claim: Two exceptions are studies of pilus-mediated autoagglutination by either TCP in the classical biotype of V. cholerae or by the DNA-uptake pilus (or, chitin-regulated pilus, ChiRP) in strain A1552 of the El Tor V. cholerae biotype.
source: To our knowledge, two exceptions are studies of pilus-mediated autoagglutination by either TCP in the classical biotype of V. cholerae or by the DNA-uptake pilus (or, chitin-regulated pilus, ChiRP) in strain A1552 of the El Tor V. cholerae biotype (Adams et al., 2018; Kirn et al., 2000; Taylor et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: V. cholerae forms communities in liquid.
source: We find that V. cholerae indeed forms communities in liquid.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Non-surface-associated V. cholerae communities are called 'aggregates' to distinguish them from the familiar V. cholerae biofilms which grow on surfaces.
source: We call these non-surface-associated V. cholerae communities 'aggregates' to distinguish them from the familiar V. cholerae biofilms which grow on surfaces.
evidence: This is a definitional statement made by the authors.

claim: Components required for V. cholerae surface-associated biofilm formation are not required for aggregate formation.
source: Mutant analyses demonstrate that components required for V. cholerae surface-associated biofilm formation are not required for aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a finding based on mutant analysis experiments.

claim: Aggregates form in the HCD QS-state.
source: Moreover, aggregates form in the HCD QS-state
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Aggregates require the HCD master regulator HapR.
source: require the HCD master regulator HapR
evidence: This is a finding based on genetic analysis.

claim: Aggregates can be driven by the addition of exogenous QS autoinducers.
source: and can be driven by the addition of exogenous QS autoinducers.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental manipulation.

claim: Surface-associated biofilm formation occurs in the LCD QS-state.
source: By contrast, surface-associated biofilm formation occurs in the LCD QS-state
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and cited work.

claim: Surface-associated biofilm formation is repressed by HapR.
source: is repressed by HapR
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and cited work.

claim: The HCD QS-state is anti-correlated with surface-biofilm formation.
source: and the HCD QS-state is anti-correlated with surface-biofilm formation (Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Aggregation occurs independently of cell growth.
source: We show that aggregation occurs independently of cell growth, again distinguishing this process from surface-associated biofilm formation.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: eDNA plays a structural role in aggregate formation.
source: We demonstrate that eDNA plays a structural role in aggregate formation
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: eDNA alone is not sufficient to induce aggregation.
source: but that eDNA alone is not sufficient to induce aggregation.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: A genetic screen identified genes including ones involved in stress response to nutrient limitation, phosphate acquisition from eDNA, and a gene unique to the current pandemic strain of V. cholerae.
source: A genetic screen to identify components required for V. cholerae aggregate formation revealed genes including ones involved in stress response to nutrient limitation, phosphate acquisition from eDNA, and, notably, a gene unique to the current pandemic strain of V. cholerae.
evidence: This is a finding based on a genetic screen.

claim: Aggregation may be a strategy employed by V. cholerae to survive under starvation conditions.
source: Combined, these results suggest that aggregation may be a strategy employed by V. cholerae to survive under starvation conditions
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The aggregation program may contribute to the pandemic potential of the current V. cholerae biotype.
source: and this program may also contribute to the pandemic potential of the current V. cholerae biotype.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Investigating V. cholerae aggregation may provide insight into how the bacterium successfully transitions between its different niches.
source: Investigating V. cholerae aggregation may provide insight into how the bacterium successfully transitions between its different niches
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of the research.

claim: Investigating V. cholerae aggregation may reveal general mechanisms underlying non-surface-dependent multicellular community formation.
source: as well as reveal general mechanisms underlying non-surface-dependent multicellular community formation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of the research.

claim: The LCD-locked strain formed clusters in liquid at 22 h.
source: The LCD-locked strain formed clusters in liquid at 22 h (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2A.

claim: LCD-locked V. cholerae cells are in a constitutive biofilm-forming state.
source: We anticipated this result because LCD-locked V. cholerae cells are in a constitutive biofilm-forming state (Hammer and Bassler, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The HCD-locked strain formed multicellular communities in liquid.
source: However, to our surprise, the HCD-locked strain also formed multicellular communities in liquid.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Aggregates formed by the HCD-locked strain were larger and morphologically distinct from the LCD-locked clusters.
source: Moreover, these aggregates were larger and morphologically distinct from the LCD-locked clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The WT strain produced aggregates morphologically similar to those formed by the HCD-locked strain.
source: The WT strain produced aggregates morphologically similar to those formed by the HCD-locked strain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2C.

claim: On surfaces, HCD-locked V. cholerae cells do not form biofilms.
source: Our finding that multicellular communities are produced by WT V. cholerae at HCD and by the HCD-locked QS strain is unexpected because on surfaces, HCD-locked V. cholerae cells do not form biofilms (Hammer and Bassler, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: VPS is essential for formation of V. cholerae surface-biofilms.
source: Essential for formation of V. cholerae surface-biofilms is VPS, a component of the extracellular matrix (Fong et al., 2010; Teschler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The ΔvpsL LCD-locked V. cholerae strain failed to form clusters.
source: The ΔvpsL LCD-locked V. cholerae strain failed to form clusters (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2D.

claim: VPS contributes to cluster formation in liquid.
source: demonstrating that VPS, in addition to driving the formation of surface-biofilms, also contributes to cluster formation in liquid.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that ΔvpsL LCD-locked strain failed to form clusters.

claim: The ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain formed aggregates similar to those made by the parent strain possessing vpsL.
source: However, the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain and the ΔvpsL WT strain formed aggregates similar to those made by the two parent strains possessing vpsL (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2D.

claim: VPS is dispensable for aggregate formation in liquid.
source: Thus, VPS is dispensable for aggregate formation in liquid.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain formed aggregates.

claim: Aggregate formation does not require initial growth on a surface.
source: Aggregate formation does not require initial growth on a surface nor is it a consequence of our sampling protocol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aggregates are finite sized.
source: and aggregates are finite sized (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: VPS-independent biofilms have been reported previously in V. cholerae O139 strain M010.
source: VPS-independent biofilms have been reported previously in V. cholerae O139 strain M010.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research.

claim: In V. cholerae O139 strain M010, in medium supplemented with oceanic Ca2+ levels, genes related to O-antigen synthesis (wbfF and wbfR) were found to be involved in development of VPS-independent surface-biofilms.
source: Specifically, in medium supplemented with oceanic Ca2+ levels, genes related to O-antigen synthesis (wbfF and wbfR) were found to be involved in development of VPS-independent surface-biofilms (Kierek and Watnick, 2003b; Kierek and Watnick, 2003a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The ΔvpsL ΔvpsN HCD-locked and the ΔvpsL ΔasnB HCD-locked mutants form aggregates as effectively as the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows that both the ΔvpsL ΔvpsN HCD-locked and the ΔvpsL ΔasnB HCD-locked mutants form aggregates as effectively as the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: vpsN and asnB do not contribute to the aggregation process.
source: Thus, vpsN and asnB do not contribute to the aggregation process we report here.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that deletion of these genes did not affect aggregation.

claim: V. cholerae O139 strain M010 is a natural variant that is locked in a LCD QS-state because of a mutation in hapR.
source: We also note that V. cholerae O139 strain M010 is a natural variant that is locked in a LCD QS-state because of a mutation in hapR (Joelsson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Removal of carR had no effect on aggregate formation in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
source: Removal of carR had no effect on aggregate formation in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The type IV TCP contributes to autoagglutination in liquid in classical V. cholerae strains.
source: Lastly, the type IV TCP and the chitin-regulated ChiRP, respectively, contribute to autoagglutination in liquid in classical V. cholerae strains and to autoaggregation in El Tor V. cholerae strain A1552 (Adams et al., 2018; Kirn et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The chitin-regulated ChiRP contributes to autoaggregation in El Tor V. cholerae strain A1552.
source: Lastly, the type IV TCP and the chitin-regulated ChiRP, respectively, contribute to autoagglutination in liquid in classical V. cholerae strains and to autoaggregation in El Tor V. cholerae strain A1552 (Adams et al., 2018; Kirn et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: No loss of aggregation occurred in ΔvpsL HCD-locked strains lacking tcpA, pilA, or mshA.
source: No loss of aggregation occurred in any case (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The aggregate formation process does not require TCP, ChiRP, or MSHA pili.
source: Thus, the aggregate formation process that we are studying here does not require these major components identified previously to control formation of multicellular communities of V. cholerae either on surfaces or in liquid.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that deletion of pilin genes did not affect aggregation.

claim: At 16 h, both the ΔvpsL WT and the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strains consisted of planktonic single cells and some small clusters, with no aggregates.
source: At 16 h, both the ΔvpsL WT and the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strains consisted of planktonic single cells and some small clusters. However, there were no aggregates (Figure 2I,M,Q,R).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2I, M, Q, R.

claim: Aggregation occurred by 19 h in the ΔvpsL WT strain.
source: Aggregation occurred by 19 h in the ΔvpsL WT strain
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: There was up to a 3 h delay in aggregation for the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain compared to the ΔvpsL WT strain.
source: and there was up to a 3 h delay in aggregation for the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Once initiated, aggregation occurred rapidly before reaching a steady state.
source: In both cases, once initiated, aggregation occurred rapidly before reaching a steady state (Figure 2J–L,N–P).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2J-L, N-P.

claim: Following the rapid onset of aggregation, only modest changes occur in volume fraction occupied by aggregates and in aggregate size distribution from T = 22–25 h.
source: Indeed, quantitation shows that, following the rapid onset of aggregation (at T = 19 h for the ΔvpsL WT strain and at T = 22 h for the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain), only modest changes occur in volume fraction occupied by aggregates (Figure 2Q) and in aggregate size distribution (Figure 2R) from T = 22–25 h.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2Q and 2R.

claim: Onset to completion of aggregation occurs within a 30 min period.
source: We found that onset to completion of aggregation occurs within a 30 min period.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from high-resolution time-course imaging.

claim: The rapidity of aggregate formation precludes a process in which cell division drives aggregate growth.
source: Importantly, the rapidity of aggregate formation precludes a process in which cell division drives aggregate growth.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed rapid kinetics of aggregation.

claim: Aggregation must be driven by a change that causes existing cells to adhere and form aggregates.
source: Rather, aggregation must be driven by a change that causes existing cells to adhere and form aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed rapid kinetics of aggregation.

claim: Growth of a mixture of equal numbers of the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain constitutively expressing either mKate2 or mTFP1 resulted in aggregates containing both red- and teal-colored cells.
source: In support of this view, growth of a mixture of equal numbers of the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain constitutively expressing either mKate2 or mTFP1 resulted in aggregates containing both red- and teal-colored cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The non-clonal nature of aggregate formation is distinct from the strictly-clonal V. cholerae surface-biofilm formation program.
source: Again, in line with our argument that this is a new community formation process, the non-clonal nature of aggregate formation is distinct from the well-established, strictly-clonal V. cholerae surface-biofilm formation program (Nadell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and experimental observation.

claim: Administration of either CAI-1 or AI-2 to the respective autoinducer-responsive strain drove aggregation.
source: Administration of either CAI-1 or AI-2 to the respective autoinducer-responsive strain drove aggregation, whereas no aggregation occurred in samples to which a solvent control was supplied (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3A.

claim: The autoinducers had no effect on aggregation if the strain to which CAI-1 or AI-2 was added lacked CqsS or LuxQ, respectively.
source: Indeed, the autoinducers had no effect on aggregation if the strain to which CAI-1 or AI-2 was added lacked CqsS or LuxQ, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence or absence of vpsL, vpsS, and cqsR did not influence responsiveness to exogenously supplied autoinducers.
source: Lastly, the presence or absence of vpsL, vpsS, and cqsR did not influence responsiveness to exogenously supplied autoinducers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CAI-1 addition between 3–6 h promoted aggregation.
source: CAI-1 addition between 3–6 h promoted aggregation
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: From 7 h onward, CAI-1 had no effect on aggregation.
source: whereas from 7 h onward, CAI-1 had no effect on aggregation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Addition of CAI-1 at late times did not simply delay the onset of aggregation.
source: Addition of CAI-1 at late times did not simply delay the onset of aggregation: at T = 46 h, cultures to which CAI-1 had been added at 7–8 h still showed no aggregation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells remain capable of detecting and controlling established QS-regulated genes in response to late-time CAI-1 supplementation.
source: Importantly, cells in our analyses remain capable of detecting and controlling established QS-regulated genes in response to late-time CAI-1 supplementation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The CAI-1-responsive strain harboring the QS-controlled luciferase genes produced maximal light at T = 22 h, independent of the time point at which CAI-1 was supplied.
source: Specifically, the CAI-1-responsive strain harboring the QS-controlled luciferase genes produced maximal light at T = 22 h, independent of the time point (0 h, 3–8 h) at which CAI-1 was supplied (Figure 3B, gray bars).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Extracellular autoinducers trigger aggregation in V. cholerae, albeit only within a specific temporal window.
source: Combined, these data show that extracellular autoinducers trigger aggregation in V. cholerae, albeit only within a specific temporal window
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations on temporal response to autoinducers.

claim: Canonical autoinducer-triggered QS-behaviors are not subject to temporal restriction.
source: while canonical autoinducer-triggered QS-behaviors are not subject to such temporal restriction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that luciferase expression responds to CAI-1 at all time points.

claim: Under the growth conditions used, T = 7 h roughly corresponds to when the cells enter stationary phase.
source: Under our growth conditions, T = 7 h, after which the aggregation phenotype becomes impervious to autoinducer supplementation, roughly corresponds to when the cells enter stationary phase.
evidence: This is an observation about the growth state of the cells.

claim: There was no difference in aggregation between the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain and the ΔvpsL ΔaphA HCD-locked strain.
source: There was no difference in aggregation between the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain and the ΔvpsL ΔaphA HCD-locked strain (Figure 3C,D,K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3C, D, K.

claim: AphA does not control aggregate formation.
source: Thus, AphA does not control aggregate formation, eliminating the first possibility.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that deletion of aphA did not affect aggregation.

claim: Deletion of hapR in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain led to a complete loss of aggregation.
source: By contrast, deletion of hapR in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain led to a complete loss of aggregation (Figure 3E,K)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3E, K.

claim: HapR is required for aggregation.
source: Thus, HapR is required for aggregation, showing that the second possibility is correct.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation that deletion of hapR eliminated aggregation.

claim: The phenotype of the ΔvpsL ΔaphA ΔhapR HCD-locked mutant strain was identical to that of the ΔvpsL ΔhapR HCD-locked mutant.
source: Indeed, epistasis analysis demonstrates that the phenotype of the ΔvpsL ΔaphA ΔhapR HCD-locked mutant strain was identical to that of the ΔvpsL ΔhapR HCD-locked mutant (Figure 3E,F,K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3E, F, K.

claim: When hapR was absent in the LCD-locked strain, no aggregation occurred.
source: When hapR was absent, no aggregation occurred (Figure 3I,K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3I, K.

claim: Deletion of aphA in the ΔvpsL LCD-locked strain led to a modest increase in aggregation.
source: We note that deletion of aphA in the ΔvpsL LCD-locked strain led to a modest increase in aggregation (Figure 3H), but one that remains below the threshold for detection by our segmentation protocol (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3H, K.

claim: AphA represses transcription of hapR.
source: AphA represses transcription of hapR (Rutherford et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Aggregation does not occur in the ΔvpsL ΔaphA ΔhapR LCD-locked strain.
source: Aggregation does not occur in the ΔvpsL ΔaphA ΔhapR LCD-locked strain (Figure 3J,K)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3J, K.

claim: The ΔvpsL ΔhapR lacZ:PhapR-hapR HCD-locked strain exhibited a comparable level of aggregation to the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain at T = 22 h.
source: At T = 22 h, the ΔvpsL ΔhapR lacZ:PhapR-hapR HCD-locked strain exhibited a comparable level of aggregation to the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: HapR is the main QS activator of aggregation.
source: We conclude that HapR is the main QS activator of aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic analysis showing HapR is required for aggregation.

claim: HapR represses dns at HCD.
source: HapR represses dns at HCD (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Xds is not known to be HapR-controlled.
source: The other extracellular nuclease, Xds, is not known to be HapR-controlled.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Both Xds and Dns nucleases contribute to the surface-biofilm program.
source: Both nucleases contribute to the surface-biofilm program (Seper et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: At 22 h, both the ΔvpsL HCD-locked and the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strains formed aggregates.
source: At 22 h, both the ΔvpsL HCD-locked and the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strains formed aggregates (Figure 4A,B,D)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4A, B, D.

claim: The average aggregate size was larger in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain than in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
source: however the average aggregate size was larger in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain than in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4F.

claim: The ΔvpsL LCD-locked and ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked strains exhibited no aggregation.
source: The ΔvpsL LCD-locked and ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked strains exhibited no aggregation (Figure 4A,C,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4A, C, E.

claim: Individual deletion of xds or dns in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain resulted in aggregation.
source: Individual deletion of xds or dns in the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain also resulted in aggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dns contributes more than Xds to overall aggregate size.
source: with Dns contributing more than Xds to overall aggregate size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The relative effects of Xds and Dns on aggregate size parallel those reported for Xds and Dns in surface-biofilm formation.
source: These relative effects parallel those reported for Xds and Dns in surface-biofilm formation (Seper et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Aggregates of the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain continued to enlarge after T = 22 h.
source: Unlike for the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain, aggregates of the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain continued to enlarge, precluding an accurate assessment of aggregate size after T = 22 h.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns lacZ:Pdns-dns HCD-locked strain produced smaller aggregates than the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain.
source: The ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns lacZ:Pdns-dns HCD-locked strain produced smaller aggregates than the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Extracellular nucleases function to limit overall aggregate size but they do not control aggregation timing.
source: We conclude that extracellular nucleases function to limit overall aggregate size but they do not control aggregation timing.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations on nuclease mutants.

claim: The concentrations of eDNA in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked and ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strains are equivalent.
source: We measured the eDNA content in all four strains at 22 h, and indeed, the concentrations of eDNA in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked and ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strains are equivalent
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: eDNA levels in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns strains are elevated ~4-fold and 10-fold compared to the ΔvpsL HCD-locked and ΔvpsL LCD-locked strains, respectively.
source: and, moreover, elevated ~4-fold and 10-fold compared to the ΔvpsL HCD-locked and ΔvpsL LCD-locked strains, respectively (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4G.

claim: By itself, accumulation of eDNA is not sufficient to drive aggregation.
source: These data show that, by itself, accumulation of eDNA is not sufficient to drive aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked strain has high eDNA but does not aggregate.

claim: Patches of eDNA were present in aggregates of the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain.
source: In the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain, patches of eDNA were present in aggregates (Figure 4H, arrow; Video 2)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4H and Video 2.

claim: A stronger eDNA signal could be visualized in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain.
source: and a stronger eDNA signal could be visualized in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain (Figure 4I, arrow; Video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4I and Video 3.

claim: DNase I treatment reduced aggregation in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain.
source: DNase I treatment reduced aggregation in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns HCD-locked strain but had little effect on the ΔvpsL HCD-locked strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: eDNA contributes to, but is not sufficient for, aggregate formation.
source: This result supports the conclusion from above that eDNA contributes to, but is not sufficient for, aggregate formation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations on eDNA and nuclease effects.

claim: eDNA plays a role in V. cholerae aggregate formation in the HCD QS-mode.
source: Combined, the data in Figure 4 show that eDNA levels are modulated through the activity of two extracellular nucleases, and eDNA, in turn, plays a role in V. cholerae aggregate formation in the HCD QS-mode.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations on eDNA and nuclease effects.

claim: There must be additional components required for V. cholerae aggregate formation beyond eDNA.
source: However, the lack of aggregate formation in the ΔvpsL Δxds Δdns LCD-locked strain, in the face of elevated eDNA levels, coupled with the finding that complete loss of aggregation does not occur upon complementation with dns or exogenous DNase I supplementation, argues that there must be additional components required for V. cholerae aggregate formation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: On agar plates, ΔvpsL HCD-locked and ΔvpsL LCD-locked colonies formed opaque and translucent colonies, respectively.
source: On agar plates, ΔvpsL HCD-locked and ΔvpsL LCD-locked colonies formed opaque and translucent colonies, respectively (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 5A, B.

claim: Variability in V. cholerae colony opacity has been previously reported.
source: Variability in V. cholerae colony opacity has been previously reported (Finkelstein et al., 1992; Finkelstein et al., 1997; Lankford, 1960)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Colony opacity has not been linked to aggregation in V. cholerae.
source: but, to our knowledge, has not been linked to aggregation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Analogous colony phenotypes are well known in other species of Vibrio, including V. parahaemolyticus and V. alginolyticus.
source: Analogous colony phenotypes are well known in other species of Vibrio, including V. parahaemolyticus and V. alginolyticus
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in related species.

claim: In V. parahaemolyticus and V. alginolyticus, opacity/translucence are QS-regulated and related to capsule synthesis.
source: and in those organisms, opacity/translucence are QS-regulated and related to capsule synthesis (Chang et al., 2009; Enos-Berlage and McCarter, 2000; Enos-Berlage et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The ΔvpsL HCD-locked V. cholerae strain, which is proficient for aggregation, forms opaque colonies.
source: Germane to our study is that the ΔvpsL HCD-locked V. cholerae strain, which is proficient for aggregation, forms opaque colonies
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Deletion of hapR results in translucent colonies, which correlates with the loss of the ability to aggregate.
source: while deletion of hapR results in translucent colonies, which correlates with the loss of the ability to aggregate (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Mutations in 12 of the 18 identified loci led to strains displaying greatly diminished aggregation.
source: Mutations in 12 of the 18 identified loci led to strains displaying greatly diminished aggregation (Table 1 reports all of the genes and from which screen they were obtained).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen.

claim: Aggregation is diminished or eliminated in all of the validated mutant strains.
source: We confirmed that aggregation is diminished or eliminated in all of the mutant strains (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Multiple insertions were identified in the operons encoding components of the TCA cycle – the succinate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes.
source: We identified multiple insertions in the operons encoding components of the TCA cycle – the succinate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes (vc2091-vc2087; sdhC, sdhD, sdhA, sdhB, and sucA)
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen.

claim: Multiple insertions were identified in the operons encoding the flagellar basal body.
source: and the flagellar basal body (vc2200-vc2198; flgBCD).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen.

claim: vca0175 is the gene responsible for the aggregation defect in the vca0175/vca0176 intergenic region.
source: In the case of the vca0175/vca0176 region, we individually deleted vca0175 and vca0176, and determined that vca0175, which has no known function, is the gene responsible for the aggregation defect.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from deletion analysis.

claim: V. cholerae forms multicellular communities in liquid that are independent of the known surface-biofilm program.
source: Here, we demonstrate the existence of an aggregation process in V. cholerae that is independent of the known surface-biofilm program.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Aggregation occurs in liquid and is rapid, suggesting that cell division is not required.
source: Aggregation occurs in liquid and is rapid, suggesting that cell division is not required.
evidence: This is a summary finding with an inference about mechanism.

claim: Aggregate formation occurs when V. cholerae cells are in a HCD QS-state, a QS-regulation pattern opposite to that for surface-biofilm formation which occurs when cells are in a LCD QS-state.
source: Aggregate formation occurs when V. cholerae cells are in a HCD QS-state, a QS-regulation pattern opposite to that for surface-biofilm formation which occurs when cells are in a LCD QS-state (Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003).
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by citations.

claim: Aggregate formation is promoted by exogenous autoinducers, although only during a limited temporal window.
source: Aggregate formation is promoted by exogenous autoinducers, although only during a limited temporal window.
evidence: This is a summary finding.

claim: HapR, the master regulator of HCD QS-behavior, is required for aggregate formation.
source: HapR, the master regulator of HCD QS-behavior, is required for aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a summary finding.

claim: eDNA is present in aggregates and contributes to overall aggregate size.
source: eDNA is present in aggregates, contributes to overall aggregate size
evidence: This is a summary finding.

claim: Two extracellular nucleases, Xds and Dns, are involved in regulating eDNA levels in aggregates.
source: and two extracellular nucleases, Xds and Dns, are involved.
evidence: This is a summary finding.

claim: For aggregate formation to occur, genes involved in stress response, phosphate uptake from eDNA, and genes of unknown function are required.
source: For aggregate formation to occur, genes involved in stress response, phosphate uptake from eDNA, genes of unknown function (including a gene, vc0175, that distinguishes the current seventh pandemic El Tor biotype from the previous classical biotype) are required.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the genetic screen.

claim: The identification of cpdB suggests that eDNA acquisition from the environment may be important for aggregate-associated cells.
source: The identification of cpdB, which is involved in phosphate acquisition from eDNA (McDonough et al., 2016), and our demonstration of Xds- and Dns-driven regulation of eDNA production in aggregates, suggests that eDNA acquisition from the environment may be important for aggregate-associated cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation and experimental findings.

claim: There is a growing recognition that bacteria form multicellular aggregates in liquid.
source: There is a growing recognition that bacteria form multicellular aggregates in liquid
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The aggregate state can confer fitness benefits including increased antibiotic resistance and improved surface-colonization relative to planktonic cells.
source: a state that, relative to individual planktonic cells, can confer fitness benefits including increased antibiotic resistance and improved surface-colonization relative to planktonic cells (Kragh et al., 2016; Kragh et al., 2018; Schleheck et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial aggregation can be modulated by factors including QS-state, eDNA, ions, and cationic polymers.
source: Bacterial aggregation can be modulated by factors including QS-state, eDNA, ions, and cationic polymers (Chandler et al., 2009; Das et al., 2014; Laganenka et al., 2016; Perez-Soto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Bacteria exhibit multicellular behaviors in the liquid-phase that are not captured by studies of surface-bound bacterial communities.
source: Combined, these findings begin to argue that bacteria exhibit multicellular behaviors in the liquid-phase that are not captured by studies of surface-bound bacterial communities.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited literature and the current study.

claim: Aggregate formation could be instrumental in the two major V. cholerae habitats—the human host and the marine environment—as well as during transitions between them.
source: We propose a model for how aggregate formation could be instrumental in the two major V. cholerae habitats—the human host and the marine environment—as well as during transitions between them.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Formation of multicellular communities occurs during human V. cholerae infection.
source: First, V. cholerae aggregation during infection: formation of multicellular communities occurs during human infection (Teschler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Filtration that removes aggregates and copepod-associated bacteria, but not planktonic cells, reduced the efficacy of V. cholerae human infections.
source: Filtration that removes aggregates and copepod-associated bacteria, but not planktonic cells, reduced the efficacy of V. cholerae human infections (Colwell et al., 2003; Huq et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of vps genes, which eliminates surface-biofilm formation in vitro, also reduced colonization in a mouse model of cholera disease.
source: Deletion of vps genes, which eliminates surface-biofilm formation in vitro, also reduced colonization in a mouse model of cholera disease (Fong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: V. cholerae exists as planktonic cells and in debris-attached aggregates in stool samples obtained from human subjects.
source: V. cholerae exists as planktonic cells and in debris-attached aggregates in stool samples obtained from human subjects (Faruque et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The ability of V. cholerae to form multicellular communities (in liquid and on surfaces) is part of its infection and dispersal process.
source: These observations suggest that the ability of V. cholerae to form multicellular communities (in liquid and on surfaces) is part of its infection and dispersal process.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited observations.

claim: During infection, following colonization of the surface of the intestinal epithelium, V. cholerae grows to abundance, enters stationary phase, and then triggers a mucosal escape program, which depends on both RpoS and HapR.
source: During infection, following colonization of the surface of the intestinal epithelium, V. cholerae grows to abundance, enters stationary phase, and then triggers a mucosal escape program, which depends on both the stationary-phase alternative sigma factor RpoS and the HCD QS-master regulator HapR (Nielsen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: It is proposed that aggregation occurs in the final stage of the infection cycle, after cells re-enter the intestinal lumen, because two conditions are met: the cells are in stationary phase and in the HCD QS-state.
source: We propose that it is in this final stage of the infection cycle, after cells re-enter the intestinal lumen, that aggregation occurs because two conditions are met: the cells are in stationary phase and in the HCD QS-state.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Formation of aggregates may allow V. cholerae a superior mechanism to survive passage through the small intestine and re-entry into the marine environment.
source: We speculate that formation of aggregates allows V. cholerae a superior mechanism (possibly by protecting aggregate-associated cells from chemical insults or by increasing intestinal transit rates) to survive passage through the small intestine and re-entry into the marine environment, where V. cholerae is immediately faced with a limited nutrient supply (Kamp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with a citation.

claim: Aggregates may determine the rate at which V. cholerae passages through the intestine.
source: Moreover, aggregates may determine the rate at which V. cholerae passages through the intestine
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Work in larval zebrafish has shown that bacterial aggregates are commonly found in the intestinal lumen and increased aggregation is correlated with elevated rates of bacterial expulsion from the intestine.
source: work in larval zebrafish, a model amenable to live imaging, has shown that bacterial aggregates are commonly found in the intestinal lumen and increased aggregation is correlated with elevated rates of bacterial expulsion from the intestine (Jemielita et al., 2014; Logan et al., 2018; Wiles et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Half of the genes identified as required for aggregation have previously been shown to be involved in V. cholerae colonization, mucosal penetration, or dissemination from the host.
source: In support of this model, we note that half of the genes (flgC, varS, sdhC, tolB, sspA, and pnp) identified here as required for aggregation have previously been shown to be involved in V. cholerae colonization, mucosal penetration, or dissemination from the host (Kamp et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2008; Merrell et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Live imaging in mice shows that multicellular V. cholerae communities are present on epithelial surfaces and these communities are clonal, while non-clonal aggregates are found in the intestinal lumen.
source: Live imaging in mice also shows that multicellular V. cholerae communities are present on epithelial surfaces and, moreover, these communities are clonal, while non-clonal aggregates are found in the intestinal lumen (Millet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: VPS-dependent surface-biofilms are clonal.
source: This finding is consistent with the observation that VPS-dependent surface-biofilms are clonal (Nadell et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Aggregates are non-clonal.
source: while we show here that aggregates are non-clonal (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The vc0175 gene, located within the VSP-I region, is required for aggregate formation.
source: Additionally, our screen identified that the vc0175 gene, located within the VSP-I region, is required for aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen.

claim: VSP-I and VSP-II are two genomic islands that distinguish the currently dominant biotype, El Tor, from the classical biotype.
source: VSP-I and VSP-II are two genomic islands that distinguish the currently dominant biotype, El Tor, from the classical biotype (Dziejman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The El Tor biotype has supplanted the classical biotype as the primary cause of the pandemic disease cholera.
source: The El Tor biotype has supplanted the classical biotype as the primary cause of the pandemic disease cholera.
evidence: This is an established fact in the field.

claim: Prior to the acquisition of VSP-I, VSP-II, the El Tor CTX prophage and several additional point mutations, the El Tor V. cholerae biotype caused infections in humans, but lacked pandemic potential.
source: Prior to the acquisition of these genomic islands, along with the El Tor CTX prophage and several additional point mutations, the El Tor V. cholerae biotype caused infections in humans, but lacked pandemic potential (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The ability to robustly form aggregates may contribute to the current dominance of the El Tor biotype.
source: Possibly, the ability to robustly form aggregates contributes to the current dominance of the El Tor biotype by making either host infection or host dispersal more productive or by increasing environmental persistence.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Aggregation could promote environmental persistence of V. cholerae by providing a mechanism for the rapid formation of multicellular communities under conditions of nutrient deprivation.
source: Now we turn to V. cholerae aggregation in its other habitat: the marine environment. Aggregation could promote environmental persistence of V. cholerae by providing a mechanism for the rapid formation of multicellular communities under conditions of nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The genetic screen identified genes with known roles in stress response or response to changes in carbon metabolism.
source: Supporting this idea, our screen identified genes (sspA, varS, sdhC, lexA, lrp, pnp) with known roles in stress response or response to changes in carbon metabolism (Brinkman et al., 2003; Butala et al., 2009; Lenz et al., 2005; Merrell et al., 2002; Romeo, 1998; Tsou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Aggregate formation might provide insight into conditionally viable environmental cells (CVEC) which are clumps of dormant environmental V. cholerae isolates.
source: With respect to the environment, aggregate formation might provide insight into conditionally viable environmental cells (CVEC; related to viable but not culturable cells (VBNC)) which are clumps of dormant environmental V. cholerae isolates that resist culturing except under very specific conditions (Alam et al., 2007; Faruque et al., 2006; Kamruzzaman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Non-clonal aggregate formation may provide V. cholerae a multicellular lifestyle amenable to horizontal gene transfer (HGT).
source: Non-clonal aggregate formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 7) may also provide V. cholerae a multicellular lifestyle amenable to horizontal gene transfer (HGT).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by experimental observation.

claim: The VPS-dependent surface-biofilm program likely cannot foster genetic diversity because V. cholerae surface-biofilms are clonal.
source: The VPS-dependent surface-biofilm program likely cannot foster genetic diversity because, as mentioned above, V. cholerae surface-biofilms are clonal (Nadell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: Expression of the genes encoding the competence machinery required for HGT is activated at HCD and in the presence of chitin.
source: Expression of the genes encoding the competence machinery required for HGT is activated at HCD and in the presence of chitin (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008; Meibom et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Aggregation could aid in the colonization of chitin surfaces and/or provide an alternative route to HGT.
source: We suggest that aggregation could aid in the colonization of chitin surfaces and/or provide an alternative route to HGT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Formation of V. cholerae aggregates during stationary phase has parallels to the spore-formation program in Myxococcus xanthus.
source: Finally, formation of V. cholerae aggregates during stationary phase has parallels to the spore-formation program in Myxococcus xanthus (Shimkets, 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by a citation.

claim: Both V. cholerae aggregation and M. xanthus spore-formation occur under conditions of starvation and require population-level collective behavior to foster community-level benefits.
source: Specifically, both processes occur under conditions of starvation and require population-level collective behavior to foster community-level benefits.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the characteristics of both processes.

claim: Aggregation might provide ecological advantages such as promoting environmental dissemination and concentrating biomass.
source: Additionally, in the case of V. cholerae, aggregation might provide ecological advantages such as promoting environmental dissemination and concentrating biomass, for example, by altering the buoyancy of the community which could aid in movement through the water column.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Aggregation is driven by surface adhesins that additionally serve in self/non-self kin-recognition.
source: We speculate that aggregation is driven by surface adhesins that additionally serve in self/non-self kin-recognition (Smukalla et al., 2008), which can defend communities against free-riders.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Kin-recognition in V. cholerae can occur via the pilins TcpA and PilA.
source: Kin-recognition in V. cholerae can occur via the pilins TcpA and PilA (Adams et al., 2018; Kirn et al., 2000; Taylor et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The aggregation process does not depend on TcpA or PilA pili.
source: While the aggregation process that we report does not depend on either of these pili (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: V. cholerae may deploy additional, as-yet undiscovered, kin-recognition systems to control its community diversity in aggregates.
source: V. cholerae may deploy additional, as-yet undiscovered, kin-recognition systems to control its community diversity in aggregates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The genetic screen identified genes required for aggregate formation, but it did not yield genes that encode obvious structural components required for V. cholerae aggregation.
source: Curiously, our screen identified genes required for aggregate formation, but it did not yield genes that encode obvious structural components required for V. cholerae aggregation.
evidence: This is an observation about the results of the genetic screen.

claim: Deeper understanding of aggregation will provide insight into whether the aggregation program is specific to V. cholerae or is more broadly conserved among bacteria.
source: We anticipate that deeper understanding will provide insight into whether the aggregation program is specific to V. cholerae or is more broadly conserved among bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Structural genes involved in V. cholerae aggregation could play analogous roles in other bacterial species.
source: Specifically, structural genes involved in V. cholerae aggregation could play analogous roles in other bacterial species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: All V. cholerae strains used were derived from a streptomycin-resistant variant of the WT O1 El Tor biotype C6706str2.
source: All V. cholerae strains used here were derived from a streptomycin-resistant variant of the WT O1 El Tor biotype C6706str2 (Thelin and Taylor, 1996).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation.

claim: Escherichia coli strain S17-1λpir was used for cloning.
source: Escherichia coli strain S17-1λpir was used for cloning.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.
